executive_summary: This assessment monitors the impact of Pratt & Whitney (RTX) powder metal contaminants on the PW1100G-JM engine fleet and the resulting Airbus A320neo aircraft-on-ground (AOG) status. Evidence from SEC filings between February and October 2026 confirms that RTX continues to manage the "Powder Metal Matter," a condition first identified in 2023 involving rare contaminants in powder metal used for specific engine parts [DOC_013, DOC_019]. These filings explicitly link the issue to increased engine removals, accelerated inspections, and elevated AOG levels for the A320neo family [DOC_019]. Additionally, FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-10360, published May 22, 2026, mandates repetitive ultrasonic inspections for crack indications on various high-pressure turbine and compressor components [DOC_018]. While the AD specifically names PW4000 series models, the underlying metallurgical analysis stems from events involving the PW1100G-JM [DOC_018]. The primary analytical takeaway is that while the technical scope of inspections is well-defined by regulators, the specific global AOG count and the precise recovery timeline for 2026 remain unquantified in available disclosures. Management should focus on reconciling these regulatory inspection cycles with Airbus delivery schedules to identify potential bottleneck shifts.
detailed_analytical_assessment:
The PW1100G-JM powder metal issue has transitioned from an emergent technical failure to a sustained regulatory and supply chain management challenge. According to RTX’s 10-K and 10-Q filings throughout 2026, the "rare condition" in powder metal requires a multi-year acceleration of the Geared Turbofan (GTF) inspection fleet [DOC_013, DOC_015, DOC_017]. The issuer acknowledges that this has resulted in "increased engine removals and inspections, shop visits, aircraft on ground levels, and costs to the Company" [DOC_019]. 

A critical development in the second quarter of 2026 was the issuance of FAA AD 2026-10360. This directive, effective June 26, 2026, requires repetitive angle ultrasonic scan inspections (AUSIs) of the HPC 15th-stage disks and HPT 1st and 2nd-stage hubs [DOC_018]. Although the AD targets PW4000 models (e.g., PW4074, PW4077), the FAA explicitly states the action was prompted by analysis of an event involving a PW1127GA-JM engine [DOC_018]. This indicates that the metallurgical risks identified in the A320neo program are driving broader regulatory scrutiny across other Pratt & Whitney engine families.

Despite these findings, significant data gaps persist. While DOC_019 confirms elevated AOG levels, it does not provide a census of grounded aircraft or a breakdown by airline. Furthermore, the "Powder Metal Matter" disclosures in late 2026 [DOC_013] repeat the 2023 discovery context without providing updated 2027-2028 compliance deadlines or specific production recovery milestones. 

The evidence suggests a high degree of confidence regarding the technical cause and the regulatory requirements for inspection. However, the downstream impact on Airbus delivery schedules is currently an analytical extrapolation rather than a documented fact. Management is advised to monitor for supplemental FAA Safety Alerts for Operators (SAFO) or Airbus-specific delivery revisions that may quantify the "increased shop visits" mentioned by RTX.

run_metadata.editor_executive_summary: This assessment monitors the impact of Pratt & Whitney (RTX) powder metal contaminants on the PW1100G-JM engine fleet and the resulting Airbus A320neo aircraft-on-ground (AOG) status. Evidence from SEC filings between February and October 2026 confirms that RTX continues to manage the "Powder Metal Matter," a condition first identified in 2023 involving rare contaminants in powder metal used for specific engine parts [DOC_013, DOC_019]. These filings explicitly link the issue to increased engine removals, accelerated inspections, and elevated AOG levels for the A320neo family [DOC_019]. Additionally, FAA Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-10360, published May 22, 2026, mandates repetitive ultrasonic inspections for crack indications on various high-pressure turbine and compressor components [DOC_018]. While the AD specifically names PW4000 series models, the underlying metallurgical analysis stems from events involving the PW1100G-JM [DOC_018]. The primary analytical takeaway is that while the technical scope of inspections is well-defined by regulators, the specific global AOG count and the precise recovery timeline for 2026 remain unquantified in available disclosures. Management should focus on reconciling these regulatory inspection cycles with Airbus delivery schedules to identify potential bottleneck shifts.
run_metadata.editor_detailed_analytical_assessment:
The PW1100G-JM powder metal issue has transitioned from an emergent technical failure to a sustained regulatory and supply chain management challenge. According to RTX’s 10-K and 10-Q filings throughout 2026, the "rare condition" in powder metal requires a multi-year acceleration of the Geared Turbofan (GTF) inspection fleet [DOC_013, DOC_015, DOC_017]. The issuer acknowledges that this has resulted in "increased engine removals and inspections, shop visits, aircraft on ground levels, and costs to the Company" [DOC_019]. 

A critical development in the second quarter of 2026 was the issuance of FAA AD 2026-10360.
